headline: GAO Finds 3 of 15 Family-Support Programs Lack Full Performance Systems
dek: The watchdog says three programs at USDA, HHS and Veterans Affairs lacked at least one core process needed to assess results and improve delivery.
entities: Department of Health and Human Services

sources.title: Federal Programs: Assessing and Improving Effectiveness

lead.creator: Pacific Southwest Region 5 / U.S. Department of Agriculture
lead.rightsBasis: Public domain: work of a U.S. Department of Agriculture employee created as part of official duties.
lead.caption: Two staff members stand outside a Head Start building. GAO reviewed performance systems in 15 federal programs serving pregnant women, young children and families.
lead.alt: Two adult staff members stand outside a Head Start program building.

charts.caption: GAO found that 12 of the 15 reviewed programs had all three core performance-management processes.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 15 programs reviewed, 12 with complete systems and three with a missing process.

charts.caption: GAO describes a cycle of setting goals, measuring progress and using evidence to improve a program.
charts.alt: Graphic lists three steps: set goals, measure progress and use evidence to improve.

paragraphs: Three of 15 federal programs reviewed by the Government Accountability Office lacked at least one core process needed to assess performance and improve results for pregnant women, children through age 5 and their families.

The other 12 programs had processes for all three parts of the performance-management cycle GAO examined: setting goals, measuring progress toward those goals and using evidence to improve program delivery.

The three programs with gaps were administered separately by the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Veterans Affairs. GAO's finding is about those specific programs, not every family-serving program at the three departments.

A missing process does not establish that a program produced no benefit. It means managers lacked part of the system needed to define intended results, track whether they were achieved or apply the findings to future decisions.

GAO said federal programs can use routine performance measures together with evaluations designed to answer deeper questions about implementation, outcomes or the contribution a program makes to observed changes.

Those evidence types serve different purposes. A performance measure can show movement over time, while a well-designed evaluation can test why results changed and whether an intervention plausibly caused the difference.

The review focused solely on 15 programs whose mission was to support the specified population. It should not be generalized to programs that serve broader populations or provide family benefits as only one part of a larger mission.

GAO's accountability concern is practical: without a complete cycle, agencies have less reliable information for deciding what to preserve, repair, expand or discontinue and for explaining those choices to Congress and the public.

The next test is whether the three programs establish the missing processes and document how the resulting evidence changes operations. Follow-up records, not the existence of a plan alone, will show whether the gaps close.
facts: GAO reviewed 15 federal programs serving pregnant women, children through age 5 and families.
Twelve programs had all three core performance-management processes.
Three programs lacked at least one core process.
The three programs were administered separately by USDA, HHS and VA.
GAO describes goal-setting, progress measurement and evidence use as the core cycle.
uncertainty: The review covers a defined set of 15 programs and is not a government-wide census.
A missing process does not by itself establish whether a program's services were effective or ineffective.
seoTitle: GAO: 3 family programs lack full performance systems
seoDescription: GAO found three of 15 federal programs for pregnant women, young children and families lacked at least one core performance process.

headline: BJS Counts 133,798 Federal Law Enforcement Officers Across 88 Agencies
dek: The 2023 census found nearly half worked in Homeland Security and seven in ten had criminal investigation as their primary function.

sources.title: Federal Law Enforcement Officers, 2023 – Statistical Tables

lead.creator: Federal Bureau of Investigation
lead.rightsBasis: Public domain: work of a Federal Bureau of Investigation employee created as part of official duties.
lead.caption: The FBI Charlotte SWAT team conducts a 2019 training exercise. BJS counted full-time federal officers authorized to make arrests and carry firearms in 2023.
lead.alt: Federal law enforcement officers participate in an outdoor training exercise.

charts.caption: BJS counted 133,798 full-time federal law enforcement officers across 88 agencies in 2023.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 133,798 officers, 88 agencies and 65,106 Homeland Security officers.

charts.caption: Criminal investigation was the primary function for 70% of officers; women were 15% of officers and 14% of supervisors.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 70 percent criminal investigation, 15 percent women officers and 14 percent women supervisors.

paragraphs: Federal agencies employed 133,798 full-time law-enforcement officers authorized to make arrests and carry firearms in 2023, according to statistical tables released by the Bureau of Justice Statistics.

The census covered 88 federal agencies. The Department of Homeland Security accounted for 65,106 officers, or 49% of the total, reflecting the size of its border, immigration, protective and investigative components.

Criminal investigation was the primary function for 70% of federal officers. The remaining officers worked principally in policing and patrol, security and protection, court operations, corrections or other functions defined in the tables.

Those categories identify a primary assignment, not every task an officer may perform. An investigator can have protective duties, and an officer assigned to security can also exercise arrest authority within a broader mission.

Women made up 15% of federal law-enforcement officers and 14% of supervisors in 2023, BJS reported. The tables provide a workforce baseline but do not by themselves explain hiring, promotion or retention patterns.

BJS reported that 57% of officers were White, 20% Hispanic or Latino and 10% Black. Other groups and records with missing or different classifications make up the remainder, so the listed shares should not be treated as a complete three-category profile.

The federal definition differs from counts of state, county, municipal or tribal officers. It also excludes employees who do not meet the report's full-time arrest-and-firearms criteria, even if they support federal enforcement work.

Because the reference year is 2023, the figures are not a live 2026 staffing roster. Agency reorganizations, hiring, departures and policy changes after the census require newer administrative records.
The release's clearest contribution is a common denominator across a fragmented system: one census of officer counts, missions and workforce characteristics that can be compared with future editions.
facts: BJS counted 133,798 full-time federal law enforcement officers in 2023.
The census covered 88 federal agencies.
DHS employed 65,106 officers, or 49% of the total.
Criminal investigation was the primary function for 70% of officers.
Women were 15% of officers and 14% of supervisors.
uncertainty: The figures describe 2023 and are not a live 2026 roster.
Primary-function categories do not capture every duty performed by an officer.
seoTitle: BJS counts 133,798 federal law enforcement officers
seoDescription: BJS counted 133,798 full-time federal law enforcement officers across 88 agencies in 2023, with 49% employed by Homeland Security.

headline: Koussevitzky Foundation Commissions Six New Works for 2026
dek: The Library of Congress announced projects by Utku Asuroglu, Pascale Criton, Malika Kishino, Reinaldo Moya, Peter S. Shin and Errollyn Wallen.

sources.title: Library Announces 2026 Music Commissions from Koussevitzky Foundation

lead.creator: Gerda Arendt
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal public-domain dedication.
lead.caption: A chamber orchestra takes applause after a 2025 concert. The Koussevitzky Music Foundation has commissioned six new works for 2026.
lead.alt: Chamber orchestra and pianist take applause on a concert-hall stage.

charts.caption: The 2026 awards commission works by six composers working with six co-sponsoring ensembles or presenters.
charts.alt: Graphic names six commissioned composers and six new works.

charts.caption: The foundation says it has commissioned 496 works since it was established.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 496 works commissioned, two Luening grants and a January 15, 2027 next deadline.

paragraphs: The Koussevitzky Music Foundation has commissioned six new works for 2026, the Library of Congress announced, extending a program that pairs composers with performing organizations.

The selected composers are Utku Asuroglu, Pascale Criton, Malika Kishino, Reinaldo Moya, Peter S. Shin and Errollyn Wallen. Each project has a co-sponsoring ensemble or presenter that is expected to bring the new work into performance.

The commission is not a single stylistic prize. The roster spans composers with different musical languages, national backgrounds and intended forces, giving the awards the practical function of placing several new scores into distinct performance networks.

Kishino and Wallen also received grants from the foundation's Vladimir and Blanche Luening Estate program. Criton received the Andrew W. Imbrie Memorial Commission, according to the Library's announcement.
Those additional designations should not be added to the six as separate commissioned composers. They are awards attached to projects within the same announced group.
The foundation was created through gifts from Serge and Natalie Koussevitzky and is administered at the Library of Congress. It says the program has commissioned 496 works since its establishment.

A commission guarantees support for creating a work, not an identical premiere schedule for every project. Completion, rehearsal and performance dates depend on the composers and co-sponsoring organizations.
For contemporary music, that partnership matters because a score's path to an audience usually requires rehearsal time, performers and a presenting institution in addition to the composer's work.

The foundation lists Jan. 15, 2027, as the next application deadline. The lasting measure of the 2026 awards will be the completed scores, their first performances and whether ensembles continue to program them.
facts: The foundation announced six 2026 commissions.
The composers are Utku Asuroglu, Pascale Criton, Malika Kishino, Reinaldo Moya, Peter S. Shin and Errollyn Wallen.
Kishino and Wallen also received Luening Estate grants.
Criton received the Andrew W. Imbrie Memorial Commission.
The foundation says it has commissioned 496 works.
uncertainty: The announcement does not provide one common premiere date for all six projects.
Future performance schedules depend on the composers and co-sponsoring organizations.
seoDescription: The Koussevitzky Music Foundation commissioned six new works for 2026, the Library of Congress announced.

headline: FDA Reopens BHT Food-Additive Comment Period Through Aug. 31
dek: The agency is seeking additional information for its post-market reassessment and says it has not reached a new safety conclusion about the preservative.

sources.title: FDA Finalizes Food Chemical Safety Post-Market Assessment Program, Launches Reassessment of BHT and ADA

lead.creator: Tessa Bury
lead.attribution: Tessa Bury / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
lead.caption: A supermarket aisle in Vermont. FDA has reopened its request for information on the food preservative BHT through Aug. 31, 2026.
lead.alt: Long supermarket aisle lined with packaged foods under bright ceiling lights.

charts.caption: FDA reopened the BHT information request through Aug. 31, 2026, under docket FDA-2026-N-2526.
charts.alt: Graphic lists August 31 deadline, docket FDA-2026-N-2526 and BHT data gathering.

charts.caption: FDA says BHT can be used in foods including cereals, frozen meals, baking mixes, cookies, gum and meat products.
charts.alt: Graphic lists cereals, frozen meals, baking mixes, cookies, gum and meat products as BHT uses.

paragraphs: The Food and Drug Administration has reopened the public-comment period for information about butylated hydroxytoluene, or BHT, through Aug. 31, 2026, as part of a post-market review of the food preservative.
The request is filed under docket FDA-2026-N-2526. FDA said it extended the opportunity after receiving requests for more time to assemble and submit information relevant to the reassessment.
The agency has not announced a new safety conclusion about BHT. A request for information is an evidence-gathering step, not a ban, recall or finding that products containing the additive are unsafe.

FDA says BHT is used to help preserve freshness in foods that can include cereals, frozen pizza and meals, baking mixes, cookies, chewing gum and meat products. Use varies by product, so the list does not mean every item in those categories contains BHT.

The reassessment is part of FDA's finalized post-market program for reviewing chemicals already used in food. Such reviews can consider new toxicology, exposure, use and manufacturing information that was unavailable when an ingredient was first evaluated.
FDA launched information gathering for both BHT and azodicarbonamide, known as ADA. It did not reopen the ADA comment period because the agency said it received no requests for additional time.

Keeping the two substances separate is important. They have different uses and evidence records, and a procedural change for the BHT docket does not establish a regulatory outcome for either chemical.

Consumers who want to know whether a packaged food contains BHT can consult the ingredient statement. The agency's population-level review is not individualized medical advice and does not replace guidance from a qualified clinician for a specific health concern.

After the comment window closes, the next public evidence will be FDA's assessment and any proposed action. Until then, the precise conclusion remains open and should not be inferred from the decision to seek more data.
facts: FDA reopened the BHT comment period through Aug. 31, 2026.
The docket is FDA-2026-N-2526.
FDA has not announced a new safety conclusion about BHT.
FDA lists several food categories in which BHT may be used.
The agency did not reopen the ADA comment period because it received no extension requests.
uncertainty: FDA's reassessment is ongoing and the regulatory outcome is not yet known.
The listed food categories do not mean every product in those categories contains BHT.
seoTitle: FDA extends BHT food-additive comments to Aug. 31
seoDescription: FDA reopened its BHT food-additive information request through Aug. 31, 2026, while stressing that reassessment remains underway.

headline: Robotic Servicer Launches to Extend Satellites in Geosynchronous Orbit
dek: The DARPA-funded vehicle carries NASA-supported robotic arms designed to inspect spacecraft and install mission-extension pods.

sources.title: Robotic Servicing Mission Launches With NASA Support

lead.creator: NASA
lead.rightsBasis: Public domain: image created solely by NASA as part of official duties.
lead.caption: Astronauts service the Hubble Space Telescope during a 2009 spacewalk. A newly launched robotic vehicle aims to perform selected servicing tasks without a crew.
lead.alt: Two astronauts in white spacesuits work on the Hubble Space Telescope above Earth.

charts.caption: The Mission Robotic Vehicle carries twin robotic arms and a NASA-supported servicing payload toward geosynchronous orbit.
charts.alt: Graphic lists one servicing vehicle, two robotic arms and a destination in geosynchronous orbit.

charts.caption: The mission is designed to inspect satellites and install mission-extension pods after reaching orbit.
charts.alt: Graphic lists inspect satellites, install extension pods and demonstrate robotic servicing.

paragraphs: A robotic servicing vehicle designed to inspect satellites and install mission-extension hardware launched July 21 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9, NASA announced.
The Mission Robotic Vehicle is traveling toward geosynchronous orbit with a NASA-supported payload known as Robotic Servicing of Geosynchronous Satellites, or RSGS.

The vehicle carries two robotic arms developed by the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory. DARPA funded the demonstration, while NASA is contributing simulation, software analysis and trained flight robot operators.

The planned work includes inspecting spacecraft and installing mission-extension pods. A successful demonstration could help satellite operators prolong useful service when a spacecraft remains functional but needs additional propulsion or related support.

The launch is the start of the mission, not proof that every planned task has succeeded. The vehicle must reach its operating orbit, complete checkout and perform its demonstrations before the technology's on-orbit performance can be judged.

Geosynchronous orbit hosts hundreds of communications, weather and other satellites. Its distance from Earth makes crewed repair far more difficult than the low-Earth-orbit servicing performed on the Hubble Space Telescope.

Robotic servicing also requires precise navigation and contact with spacecraft that may not have been designed for repair. Demonstrations must show that the arms, software and operators can work without damaging the client satellite.
The mission is not a general rescue guarantee for every aging spacecraft. Compatibility, ownership, operational approvals and the condition of a target all affect whether servicing is feasible.

The decisive evidence will come after arrival: checkout results, documented servicing demonstrations and measurements of whether installed hardware extends a satellite's useful operations as intended.
facts: The Mission Robotic Vehicle launched July 21, 2026, on a SpaceX Falcon 9.
It is traveling toward geosynchronous orbit.
The vehicle carries two robotic arms developed by the Naval Research Laboratory.
DARPA funded the demonstration and NASA provides operational support.
Planned tasks include satellite inspection and installation of mission-extension pods.
uncertainty: Launch does not establish that the on-orbit servicing demonstrations will succeed.
Not every satellite is compatible with or eligible for robotic servicing.
seoTitle: Robotic satellite servicer launches for geosynchronous orbit
seoDescription: A DARPA-funded robotic satellite servicer launched with NASA support to inspect spacecraft and install mission-extension pods in geosynchronous orbit.

headline: State and Local Pension Assets Reached $6.49 Trillion in 2025
dek: Census Bureau data show an 8.46% increase in assets, more than 37 million participants and $418.25 billion in benefit payments.

lead.creator: Downtowngal
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported; derivative crops distributed under the same license.
lead.caption: Los Angeles public-works employees resurface a street. Census data cover retirement systems serving more than 37 million state and local participants.
lead.alt: Municipal public-works crew operates paving equipment on a city street.

charts.caption: State and local pension assets rose from $5.98 trillion in 2024 to $6.49 trillion in 2025.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 5.98 trillion dollars in 2024, 6.49 trillion in 2025 and an 8.46 percent increase.

charts.caption: Systems reported $315.02 billion in contributions and $418.25 billion in benefit payments during 2025.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 315.02 billion dollars in contributions, 418.25 billion in benefits and more than 37 million participants.

paragraphs: State and local government retirement systems held $6.49 trillion in assets in 2025, an 8.46% increase from $5.98 trillion a year earlier, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.

The systems covered more than 37 million members, beneficiaries and other participants. That total spans active workers, retirees and people with different benefit statuses rather than 37 million current employees.
Contributions totaled $315.02 billion during the year. Employees supplied 24.83% of contributions and governments supplied 75.17%, the Census Bureau reported.

Benefit payments reached $418.25 billion, up 3.40% from $404.46 billion in 2024. Contributions and benefit payments are annual flows, while the $6.49 trillion asset figure is a year-end stock, so they should not be compared as if they were the same measure.

Asset growth can reflect investment returns, contributions, payments and changes in the systems included or reported. The national total does not show that every state or local plan improved by the same percentage.

Likewise, a large asset balance is not a complete measure of pension health. Funding adequacy depends on promised benefits, actuarial assumptions, contribution policy, workforce demographics and the timing of future payments.
The annual survey provides a consistent national view across state and local systems, making it useful for tracking the scale and direction of public retirement finances over time.

It does not provide individualized retirement guidance. A participant's benefit depends on the rules and records of the specific system, while fiscal judgments require plan-level liabilities and actuarial reports.

The next comparison will show whether asset gains persisted and how contributions and benefit payments changed. Plan-level records remain necessary to understand risks hidden by the national aggregate.
facts: State and local pension assets totaled $6.49 trillion in 2025.
Assets increased 8.46% from $5.98 trillion in 2024.
The systems covered more than 37 million participants.
Contributions totaled $315.02 billion.
Benefit payments totaled $418.25 billion, up 3.40%.
uncertainty: National asset growth does not establish the funded status of any individual plan.
Funding adequacy requires plan-level liabilities, assumptions and actuarial records not summarized by the asset total.
seoTitle: State and local pension assets hit $6.49T in 2025
seoDescription: Census data show state and local pension assets reached $6.49 trillion in 2025, up 8.46%, with more than 37 million participants.
